name: Serenna veriformans
habitat: Understorey shrub, filtered light, well-drained volcanic soil
distribution: Cultivated on Isla Nublar; ornamental planting throughout the guest circulation route
growth: Dense shrub to 2 m with broad opposing leaves and pale inflorescence
toxicity: Severe. Whole plant contains a cardiac glycoside; berries are lethal to humans in small quantity.
ecologicalRole: Understorey coloniser. Unpalatable to every herbivore asset tested, giving it a competitive advantage in browsed enclosures.
reconstruction: Recovered from amber-preserved pollen. Genome closed with modern Apocynaceae sequence.
researchValue: Moderate botanically, high institutionally. This is the plant that established the archive's position on ornamental toxicity.
notes: Planted along the 1993 tour route on aesthetic grounds without a toxicity review. The species was known to be lethal at the time of planting and was specified anyway. Every later planting decision requires botanical sign-off because of this record.

name: Cycadeoidea
habitat: Open woodland margins, seasonally dry soils
distribution: Established on Isla Nublar and Isla Sorna; naturalised in the Sorna interior basin
growth: Squat barrel trunk to 1.5 m bearing a crown of stiff pinnate fronds; extremely slow growing
toxicity: Moderate. Seeds contain cycasin analogues; chronic ingestion causes hepatic damage in mammals.
ecologicalRole: Primary browse for low-feeding herbivore assets. Slow regeneration makes it vulnerable to sustained grazing pressure.
reconstruction: Assembled from unusually complete amber-preserved cone material. One of the earliest successful plant reconstructions.
researchValue: High. The reconstruction predates the first viable animal asset and proved the pipeline worked on plant tissue first.
notes: Overgrazed to near-elimination in the Nublar enclosures within four years, which produced the browse-rotation model used in every later paddock. The Sorna population, unmanaged, is stable.

name: Araucaria mirabilis
habitat: Canopy conifer, volcanic soils, high rainfall
distribution: Canopy plantings on both islands; dominant in the Sorna interior tree line
growth: Columnar conifer exceeding 45 m at maturity with spirally arranged scale leaves and heavy woody cones
toxicity: None recorded. Resin is a contact irritant in quantity.
ecologicalRole: Canopy structure and high browse. Cones are a seasonal food source for large herbivore assets.
reconstruction: Reconstructed from silicified cone material rather than amber — one of few records not dependent on the amber pipeline.
researchValue: High. Provides the vertical structure the large-herbivore enclosures required to read as habitat rather than paddock.
notes: The most successful plant introduction in the programme. Growth rates on Sorna exceeded projection by a wide margin, and the species now forms the structural canopy of an ecosystem InGen no longer manages.

name: Ancestral Tree Fern
habitat: Shaded gullies, stream margins, high humidity
distribution: Widespread on both islands; heavy planting through the 1993 tour route
growth: Fibrous trunk to 5 m topped by a crown of fronds up to 3 m
toxicity: None. Frond hairs cause mild mechanical irritation.
ecologicalRole: Understorey humidity retention and ground cover. Provides visual screening between enclosure and guest sightline.
reconstruction: Not reconstructed. An extant lineage selected for archaic morphology and cultivated as period-appropriate planting.
researchValue: Low scientifically. High operationally as fast-establishing screening cover.
notes: Included in the archive despite requiring no genetic work, because it occupies more planted area than any reconstructed species. Roughly a third of the visible vegetation in the 1993 park was never extinct at all.

name: Bennettitalean Composite BC-4
habitat: Open scrub, poor soils, high light
distribution: Contained plots at Site B only. Never released to open planting.
growth: Branching shrub to 3 m with flower-like reproductive structures
toxicity: Unassessed. Pollen provokes a severe respiratory response in exposed personnel.
ecologicalRole: Unknown in practice. Never established outside containment.
reconstruction: Composite. Fragmentary source material from three separate amber deposits, closed with modern gymnosperm and angiosperm sequence.
researchValue: High and unresolved. The reproductive structures do not match any accepted reconstruction of the group.
notes: The lowest genome completion of any cultivated plant record, and the composite sequence makes it impossible to say which features are recovered and which are artefacts of the closure method. Retained under containment pending review that has not been scheduled since 1995.

name: Giant Horsetail
habitat: Saturated ground, river margins, standing water
distribution: Naturalised throughout the Sorna river system and the Nublar drainage
growth: Jointed hollow stems to 5 m forming dense colonial stands
toxicity: Low. Contains thiaminase; sustained ingestion causes deficiency in mammals.
ecologicalRole: Bank stabilisation and wetland structure. Colonises disturbed ground quickly.
reconstruction: Extant lineage, selected for size and archaic morphology.
researchValue: Low. Included for its behaviour as an invasive rather than its biology.
notes: Introduced for bank stabilisation and spread well beyond specification. It now dominates the Sorna river margins to the exclusion of planted species, and no control programme was ever attempted.

name: Ancestral Ginkgo
habitat: Riparian woodland, disturbed ground, temperate to subtropical
distribution: Specimen plantings at both island sites and the Palo Alto campus
growth: Deciduous tree to 30 m with fan-shaped leaves and fleshy malodorous seed coats
toxicity: Low. Seed coat contains a contact allergen; kernels are toxic in quantity.
ecologicalRole: Riparian canopy. Seeds are taken opportunistically by small herbivore assets.
reconstruction: Recovered from compression fossil material with an unusually intact chloroplast genome; closed against extant Ginkgo biloba.
researchValue: High. The closest thing in the archive to a control: the extant relative is near-identical, allowing reconstruction error to be measured directly.
notes: The highest genome completion of any record in this division, and the only one where the reconstruction can be checked against a living organism. Used as the calibration reference for the plant pipeline.

name: Wollemi Pine
habitat: Sheltered sandstone gorges; cultivated in filtered light
distribution: Limited ornamental planting on Isla Nublar; specimen trees at the Biosyn valley complex
growth: Multi-stemmed conifer to 25 m with bubbled bark and two-ranked foliage
ecologicalRole: Minor canopy component. Not browsed by any asset on record.
reconstruction: None required. A living species, extremely rare in the wild, cultivated for period-appropriate appearance.
researchValue: Low botanically. Cited internally as precedent that a species can survive unchanged for a hundred million years without intervention.
notes: The park's marketing repeatedly described this as a de-extincted species. It was never extinct. The claim was not corrected because nobody asked.

name: Sago Cycad — Paddock Cultivar
distribution: Standard planting in every Jurassic World herbivore enclosure
growth: Stiff crown of pinnate fronds on a short trunk; regenerates readily from the base after browsing
toxicity: High. Contains cycasin; ingestion causes hepatic failure in mammals. Herbivore assets are unaffected.
ecologicalRole: Regenerating browse. Selected specifically for recovery rate after grazing.
reconstruction: None. Selectively cultivated from extant stock for browse tolerance.
researchValue: Low scientifically, high operationally. Solved the enclosure defoliation problem that Cycadeoidea created.
notes: The practical answer to a problem the reconstructed cycad caused. Keepers were briefed on the toxicity risk to themselves and to guests; no incident is recorded.

name: Microvictoria
habitat: Still fresh water, shallow margins, high light
distribution: Ornamental water features on Isla Nublar; drainage ponds on Isla Sorna
growth: Floating leaves to 30 cm with nocturnal flowers that trap pollinating beetles overnight
ecologicalRole: Freshwater surface cover and beetle pollination cycle. Establishes rapidly in still water.
reconstruction: Recovered from exceptionally preserved amber floral material. Reconstruction of the beetle-trapping mechanism was inferred, not observed.
researchValue: High. The pollination behaviour appeared exactly as inferred, validating a functional prediction made from morphology alone.
notes: The strongest evidence in this division that reconstruction recovers behaviour and not merely form. The flower does something nobody had ever seen it do, precisely as predicted.

name: Pachypteris
distribution: Coastal plantings on both islands, particularly exposed windward slopes
growth: Low sprawling shrub to 1.2 m with thick waxy pinnate foliage
toxicity: None recorded. Foliage is unpalatable rather than toxic.
ecologicalRole: Coastal stabilisation and salt-spray tolerance where nothing else establishes.
reconstruction: Assembled from carbonised coastal deposits with amber-derived closure.
researchValue: Moderate. Salt tolerance exceeds all modern comparators tested and is under separate agricultural review.
notes: The only record in this division with a commercial application outside the parks. The salt-tolerance mechanism was flagged for agricultural licensing in 2009; no licence was ever issued.
